questions.q: A particle's position is given by $\vec{r}(t)=\langle t^2, t^3\rangle$. Find the velocity vector $\vec{v}(t)$ and acceleration vector $\vec{a}(t)$.
For the same particle, find the speed at $t=2$.
Given $\vec{v}(t)=\langle3t^2,2t\rangle$ and initial position $\vec{r}(0)=\langle1,4\rangle$, find $\vec{r}(t)$.
A particle has velocity $\vec{v}(t)=\langle\cos t,\sin t\rangle$ for $t\in[0,\pi]$. Find the total distance traveled.
A particle moves along $x(t)=e^t$, $y(t)=e^{-t}$. Find the velocity vector and speed at $t=0$.
For the particle above, find the magnitude of the acceleration vector at $t=0$.
For $\vec{r}(t)=\langle t,t^2\rangle$, find the unit tangent vector $\vec{T}(t)$ at $t=1$.
Explain why $\vec{T}(t)=\frac{\vec{v}(t)}{|\vec{v}(t)|}$ always has magnitude $1$.
questions.answer: Dividing any nonzero vector by its own magnitude produces a vector with magnitude $\frac{|\vec{v}(t)|}{|\vec{v}(t)|}=1$ by definition — this is the standard construction of a unit vector in the same direction.

sections.heading: Motion on a circle and centripetal acceleration

questions.q: A particle moves along $\vec{r}(t)=\langle3\cos t, 3\sin t\rangle$. Find $\vec{v}(t)$, $\vec{a}(t)$, and verify that $\vec{a}(t)$ points toward the origin (is a scalar multiple of $-\vec{r}(t)$).
questions.answer: $\vec{v}(t)=\langle-3\sin t,3\cos t\rangle$. $\vec{a}(t)=\langle-3\cos t,-3\sin t\rangle=-\vec{r}(t)$. Since $\vec{a}(t)$ is exactly $-1$ times $\vec{r}(t)$, it points directly toward the origin (centripetal acceleration).

questions.q: For the same particle, verify that $\vec{v}(t)\cdot\vec{r}(t)=0$ for all $t$, and interpret this geometrically.
questions.answer: $\vec{v}(t)\cdot\vec{r}(t)=(-3\sin t)(3\cos t)+(3\cos t)(3\sin t)=-9\sin t\cos t+9\sin t\cos t=0$. This confirms the velocity vector is always perpendicular to the position vector — consistent with circular motion, where velocity is tangent to the circle.

sections.heading: Displacement vs. distance for vector motion

questions.q: A particle has position $\vec{r}(t)=\langle t^2,t\rangle$ for $t\in[0,2]$. Find the displacement vector from $t=0$ to $t=2$.
Set up (but do not evaluate) the integral for the total distance traveled by the particle $\vec{r}(t)=\langle t^2,t\rangle$ over $t\in[0,2]$.
Given $\vec{u}=\langle3,-2\rangle$ and $\vec{w}=\langle-1,4\rangle$, find $2\vec{u}-3\vec{w}$.
Find the dot product $\vec{u}\cdot\vec{w}$ for $\vec{u}=\langle3,-2\rangle$ and $\vec{w}=\langle-1,4\rangle$, and state whether the vectors are perpendicular.
questions.answer: $\vec{u}\cdot\vec{w}=3(-1)+(-2)(4)=-3-8=-11$. Since the dot product is not $0$, the vectors are NOT perpendicular.

questions.q: A particle moves along $\vec{r}(t)=\langle t^3,t^2\rangle$. Find the times $t$ when the particle's speed is exactly $\sqrt{13}$.
questions.answer: $\vec{v}(t)=\langle3t^2,2t\rangle$. Speed$^2=9t^4+4t^2=13$. Let $w=t^2$: $9w^2+4w-13=0$. Using the quadratic formula: $w=\frac{-4\pm\sqrt{16+468}}{18}=\frac{-4\pm22}{18}$. Taking the positive root: $w=1$, so $t^2=1 \Rightarrow t=\pm1$.

questions.q: For the particle $\vec{r}(t)=\langle t,\ln t\rangle$ ($t>0$), find the velocity vector and speed at $t=1$.

sections.heading: Projectile motion as a vector-valued function

questions.q: A projectile is launched with position $\vec{r}(t)=\langle 20t, 30t-4.9t^2\rangle$ (meters, seconds). Find the velocity vector $\vec{v}(t)$ and the time when the projectile reaches maximum height (where the vertical velocity component is $0$).
questions.answer: $\vec{v}(t)=\langle20,30-9.8t\rangle$. Maximum height occurs when $30-9.8t=0 \Rightarrow t=\frac{30}{9.8}\approx3.06$ s.

questions.q: For the same projectile, find the speed at $t=0$ (launch) and interpret its two components.
questions.answer: $\vec{v}(0)=\langle20,30\rangle$. Speed $=\sqrt{20^2+30^2}=\sqrt{400+900}=\sqrt{1300}\approx36.1$ m/s. The horizontal component ($20$ m/s) stays constant throughout the flight, while the vertical component ($30$ m/s initially) decreases due to gravity.

sections.heading: Finding when a particle is at rest

questions.q: A particle moves along $\vec{r}(t)=\langle t^3-3t,\, t^2-4\rangle$. Find all times $t$ when the particle is momentarily at rest (both velocity components equal $0$ simultaneously).
questions.answer: $\vec{v}(t)=\langle3t^2-3,2t\rangle$. Need $3t^2-3=0$ AND $2t=0$ simultaneously. From the second equation, $t=0$; check the first: $3(0)^2-3=-3\neq0$. There is NO time when both components are zero at once, so the particle is never fully at rest.

questions.q: For the same particle, find the times when only the horizontal velocity component is $0$.
State the arc length formula for a vector-valued function $\vec{r}(t)=\langle x(t),y(t)\rangle$ on $[a,b]$, and explain how it relates to the speed $|\vec{v}(t)|$.
questions.answer: $L=\int_a^b|\vec{v}(t)|\,dt=\int_a^b\sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2+\left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}\,dt$ — arc length is the integral of speed over time, which matches the intuition that distance traveled equals the accumulated speed.

questions.answer: $\vec{v}(t)=\langle3t^2-12,2t\rangle$. Setting $3t^2-12=0$: $t^2=4 \Rightarrow t=\pm2$. The positive value is $2$.

questions.q: A particle moves along $\vec{r}(t)=\langle t^3-108t,t^2+3\rangle$. Find the positive time $t$ when the horizontal velocity component is $0$.
questions.answer: $\vec{v}(t)=\langle3t^2-108,2t\rangle$. Setting $3t^2-108=0$: $t^2=36 \Rightarrow t=\pm6$. The positive value is $6$.

questions.q: A particle moves along $\vec{r}(t)=\langle t^3-48t,t^2+3\rangle$. Find the positive time $t$ when the horizontal velocity component is $0$.
questions.answer: $\vec{v}(t)=\langle3t^2-48,2t\rangle$. Setting $3t^2-48=0$: $t^2=16 \Rightarrow t=\pm4$. The positive value is $4$.

questions.q: A particle moves along $\vec{r}(t)=\langle t^3-12t,t^2-6\rangle$. Find the positive time $t$ when the horizontal velocity component is $0$.
questions.answer: $\vec{v}(t)=\langle3t^2-12,2t\rangle$. Setting $3t^2-12=0$: $t^2=4 \Rightarrow t=\pm2$. The positive value is $2$.

questions.q: A particle moves along $\vec{r}(t)=\langle t^3-75t,t^2+3\rangle$. Find the positive time $t$ when the horizontal velocity component is $0$.
